title: Pope Leo and artificial intelligence
text:
Pope Leo offered his ideas by issuing a kind of document known as an encyclical, a nearly 400-year-old papal tradition of teaching the Roman Catholic faithful. The document was issued on Monday, titled “Magnifica Humanitas,” or “Magnificent Humanity.” (see below for a link to the full text).

Wow! I am struggling to understand and make sense of our collective angst at AI and fears of displacement and what it signals for humanity.  The pontiff writes: “The primary choice is not between a âyes’ or âno’ to technology, but rather between constructing Babel or rebuilding Jerusalem,” he wrote. 

In the Bible, the Tower of Babel symbolizes a top-down, grandiose project where decisions are driven by pride, profit and a push for homogenization, the pope suggested in his text. In the rebuilding of Jerusalem, diverse people worked together to rebuild the ruined walls and established a fraternal coexistence within them, he added.

I completely appreciate and support the motivation by the pontiff: to provide humanism and safety for global benefit and warn against the risks of uncontrolled forces and negative motivations.

At its strongest, the pope is identifying something many technologists themselves privately admit: AI is not merely a neutral tool. It is an economic and political force capable of concentrating power, reshaping labor markets, mediating human relationships, and redefining what counts as knowledge or creativity. His warning that humans risk becoming “mere cogs in a system driven toward ever greater efficiency” echoes long-standing critiques from labor theory, existential philosophy, and even Silicon Valley dissidents themselves.

Whether one agrees or disagrees, the pope deserves credit for recognizing that AI is not simply a technological upgrade. It is potentially a civilizational turning point. The weakness of the statement is not that it is alarmist, but that it still assumes ethical persuasion and regulation can meaningfully steer systems driven by immense geopolitical competition, military incentives, and trillion-dollar market forces.

The unanswered question is whether moral institutions still possess enough authority to shape technological civilization—or whether they are now commentators watching events unfold from the sidelines.

But there are several important critiques of the pope’s framing.

First, the encyclical risks romanticizing “humanity” without defining what specifically makes human cognition morally superior in all domains. Human beings themselves are not paragons of wisdom, empathy, or justice. Humans generate propaganda, wage wars, exploit labor, and manipulate each other at scale without AI assistance. One could argue that some AI systems may eventually reduce certain forms of human cruelty or irrationality rather than amplify them. The pope warns against “anti-human” visions, but history shows that many deeply anti-human systems were entirely human-created and human-operated.

Second, there is a danger of treating AI primarily as a moral problem rather than also an economic inevitability. The encyclical emphasizes regulation and ethical oversight, which are reasonable, but it underestimates geopolitical dynamics. If democratic nations slow AI development while authoritarian states aggressively pursue it, the result may not be safer AI but strategic imbalance. This is the core argument of many techno-optimists and national security thinkers. The pope gestures toward this tension but largely avoids confronting the possibility that restraint itself carries risks.

Third, the Vatican’s position contains an unresolved contradiction regarding centralized authority. The Church critiques concentrated technological power while itself being one of history’s oldest hierarchical institutions claiming moral authority over universal human questions. Critics may ask why ecclesiastical authority should be considered less dangerous than technological authority. The difference, the Church would argue, is that moral authority aims to preserve human dignity while technocratic authority optimizes efficiency and control. But that distinction depends heavily on trust in institutions that many modern people no longer share.

Another interesting tension is the Vatican’s engagement with companies like Anthropic while simultaneously criticizing the structures that created them. The inclusion of Christopher Olah suggests the Church recognizes it cannot remain outside technological development and merely condemn it from afar. Yet this creates the risk of symbolic co-option: tech firms gain moral legitimacy simply by participating in dialogue with religious institutions.

We will be talking about all this for years to come. I appreciate the Pope to take a position on this, as his voice will elevate this issue across the globe, regardless of your personal belief system!

History of prior Encyclicals by the Church:
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/25/world/europe/pope-leo-encyclical-ai.html
1. On Workers’ Rights: “Rerum Novarum”
2. On World Peace: “Pacem in Terris”
3. On Birth Control: “Humanae Vitae”
4. On Economics: “Caritas in Veritate”
5. On the Environment: “Laudato Si’”

Full text of the current Encyclical (which means Peace on Earth).

https://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/encyclicals/documents/20260515-magnifica-humanitas.html
